heuristics.rule: RSU from established public companies: hold until vested, then decide when to sell — no action required before vesting
heuristics.condition: When you receive RSU from a public company (Google, Facebook, Apple, etc.)
heuristics.action: Wait for vesting events, then sell during open trading windows; no upfront capital required
heuristics.because: RSU converts directly to stock at vesting with no purchase required — the only decision is when to sell, not whether to buy

heuristics.rule: For NSO stock options at a startup that IPOs, exercise incrementally each year to stay in a lower income tax bracket rather than exercising all at once
heuristics.condition: When a startup with NSO options goes public and you hold a large number of vested options
heuristics.action: Exercise a portion each tax year rather than all at once to control taxable income and potentially apply a lower marginal rate
heuristics.because: The post explicitly notes that exercising fewer options in one year can drop you into a lower tax bracket — approximately 4% savings in marginal rate

heuristics.rule: Treat ISO early exercise with extreme caution unless you are an early-stage employee with a very low strike price
heuristics.condition: When offered ISO options at a startup with early exercise rights
heuristics.action: Consult a tax professional before early exercising; do not act on ISO options without understanding AMT exposure
heuristics.because: The 2000 dot-com bubble produced mass bankruptcies among employees who early-exercised ISO options and were hit with AMT tax on paper gains that later evaporated

decision_factors.factor: Equity instrument type: RSU vs. NSO vs. ISO
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Each type has a fundamentally different tax treatment and risk profile — RSU taxes as ordinary income at vest, NSO taxes as ordinary income at exercise, ISO can trigger AMT
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check the offer letter or equity agreement for the explicit label (RSU, NSO, ISO); do not assume — ask HR or legal

decision_factors.factor: Company stage: public vs. pre-IPO startup
decision_factors.why_it_matters: RSU from a pre-IPO company is illiquid and untaxable until a liquidity event; options at a startup may never be worth anything if IPO/acquisition doesn't occur
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Determine whether the company is publicly traded, has a clear IPO timeline, or is in a high-valuation unicorn category

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Non-standard vesting schedules (e.g., Amazon 5:15:40:40, Snapchat 10:20:30:40) heavily back-load value, meaning early departure yields far less than a standard 1-year cliff + monthly schedule
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Read the vesting schedule in the offer letter explicitly; calculate the value you'd receive if you left at 1 year, 2 years, 3 years

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Standard 90-day exercise window forces you to either pay to exercise options immediately upon leaving or forfeit them; longer windows (7-10 years) remove this pressure
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check the option agreement for the post-termination exercise window; compare against industry norm of 90 days

decision_factors.factor: State of residence for tax purposes
decision_factors.why_it_matters: California state income tax adds a significant additional tax burden (~13.3% top rate) on top of federal tax when RSU vests or options are exercised
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Determine whether you are working in a state with income tax (California being the most impactful) vs. a no-income-tax state (Texas, Washington)

decision_factors.factor: Strike price relative to current fair market value
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Options with a strike price close to the current valuation have low intrinsic value and require significant appreciation to be worthwhile; early employees get much lower strike prices
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask for the current 409A valuation and compare it to your strike price; calculate the upside needed to profit after taxes

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a large RSU grant from a pre-IPO startup
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: At IPO, the entire accumulated unvested RSU value is taxed as ordinary income in a single year, potentially pushing the employee into the highest tax bracket — effectively losing ~50% of the grant value to taxes
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Employees who joined a startup years before IPO and have accumulated a large RSU balance

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Early exercising ISO options at a startup
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: If the company's stock later drops (as in the 2000 dot-com crash), the employee still owes AMT (Alternative Minimum Tax) calculated on the paper gain at exercise time, even though the stock is now worthless — leading to tax bills exceeding the actual value of shares held
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Employees at high-growth startups who early-exercise ISO options anticipating IPO gains

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Leaving a startup before options vest
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Standard 90-day exercise window after departure forces an immediate cash decision: pay the full strike price plus anticipated tax, or forfeit all vested options
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Employees at startups with standard short exercise windows, especially those who have vested options with significant spread but limited personal liquidity

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Prioritizing base salary over equity when evaluating offers
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: In Silicon Valley/Bay Area tech, the compounding upside of equity — especially at pre-IPO companies — can dwarf total base salary over a multi-year period; optimizing for base salary alone can mean leaving very large sums on the table
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: New graduates and international candidates who focus on the certainty of base pay and discount equity as speculative

failure_patterns.pattern: Focusing exclusively on base salary when comparing offers, ignoring equity structure differences
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Base salary is concrete, immediate, and easy to compare; equity requires understanding vesting, strike prices, tax treatment, and liquidity — all of which feel uncertain and complex
failure_patterns.consequence: Candidates make regrettable decisions — choosing a slightly higher salary over meaningfully more valuable equity at a better-positioned company
warning_signs: Candidate says 'I just want a stable salary, the stock stuff is too complicated'
Candidate compares offers by base salary alone without modeling equity value scenarios

failure_patterns.pattern: Early exercising ISO options without understanding AMT exposure
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Employees are told early exercise is a tax optimization strategy (start the capital gains clock early); they act without modeling the AMT liability under different stock price scenarios
failure_patterns.consequence: If the stock price drops post-exercise, the employee holds worthless or low-value stock but still owes AMT calculated on the original paper gain — the mechanism behind thousands of 2000-era bankruptcies
warning_signs: Employee exercises ISO options at a paper gain but does not immediately sell shares
Employee does not consult a tax professional before exercising

failure_patterns.pattern: Treating equity grants as certain income when a company has not yet IPO'd or been acquired
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The nominal dollar value in the offer letter feels real; candidates anchor to it and factor it into lifestyle decisions
failure_patterns.consequence: If the company fails to IPO or be acquired, RSU and options are worth zero — employees who made financial decisions based on expected equity value suffer significant losses
warning_signs: Candidate says 'I'm getting $500K in RSU' about a pre-IPO company as if it is cash
Candidate declines a public company offer in favor of a startup primarily because of the stated RSU value

diagnostic_questions.question: Is the equity grant RSU or Stock Options — and if options, is it ISO or NSO?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: The tax treatment and risk profile are entirely different; the question surfaces whether the candidate understands what they are actually receiving
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If RSU: is the company public? If not, when is the expected liquidity event?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If options: what is the strike price, current 409A valuation, and post-termination exercise window?

diagnostic_questions.question: What is the vesting schedule, and does it follow the standard 1-year cliff + monthly, or is it back-loaded like Amazon or Snapchat?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Back-loaded schedules dramatically reduce value if you leave before year 3-4; a back-loaded schedule is effectively a retention trap that punishes early departure
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If back-loaded: model the value you receive at each year mark and compare against a standard schedule
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If standard: verify the total grant value and whether there is a refresh grant policy after the initial 4-year cliff

diagnostic_questions.question: If this is a pre-IPO startup, what is the realistic liquidity scenario and timeline?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Without a credible path to IPO or acquisition, the equity has no liquidity and effectively zero near-term value regardless of the stated valuation
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If there is a realistic IPO path: estimate post-IPO lockup period and tax bill on accumulated RSU/options
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If no clear liquidity path: treat the equity as speculative and evaluate the offer based primarily on cash compensation

diagnostic_questions.question: How long is the exercise window after leaving the company?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: A standard 90-day window creates enormous pressure and may force forfeiture of vested options if you cannot afford the strike price plus anticipated tax; longer windows are a meaningful benefit
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If 90 days: calculate whether you could afford to exercise all vested options if you left today
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If extended (2+ years or 10 years): this is a significant pro-employee benefit that reduces the lock-in effect of options

industry_realities.common_belief: Equity compensation from tech companies is essentially free money on top of your salary
industry_realities.actual_reality: RSU vesting is a taxable event at ordinary income rates; in California, combined federal + state tax can consume ~40-50% of the vested value immediately, and ISO options carry potential AMT liability that can exceed the actual cash value of the shares
industry_realities.implication: Candidates should model after-tax equity value — not gross grant value — when comparing offers; the stated RSU value in an offer letter is not what you will actually receive

industry_realities.common_belief: Stock options are always better than RSU because they have more upside
industry_realities.actual_reality: Options require capital outlay to exercise, carry more complex tax exposure (especially ISO/AMT), expire after departure (often 90 days), and are worth zero if the stock doesn't rise above the strike price; RSU have lower ceiling but guaranteed value as long as the stock has any value
industry_realities.implication: For employees who are not early-stage founders or very early employees, RSU is often the lower-risk, more predictable form of equity compensation; options are higher variance in both directions

industry_realities.common_belief: Pre-IPO RSU and post-IPO RSU work the same way
industry_realities.actual_reality: Pre-IPO RSU typically has a double-trigger vesting condition (time + liquidity event); if the company never IPOs or is acquired, vested RSU cannot be converted to cash regardless of how long you've waited
industry_realities.implication: Pre-IPO RSU should be evaluated as contingent compensation with significant binary risk, not as the equivalent of deferred cash

industry_realities.common_belief: You can always choose to not exercise options if the stock price drops, so options carry no downside risk
industry_realities.actual_reality: With ISO options that have already been early-exercised (or in any scenario where AMT has been triggered), the tax liability is not contingent on the stock's future value — you can owe taxes on gains that no longer exist
industry_realities.implication: The 'worst case is zero' framing only applies cleanly to unexercised NSO options; ISO early-exercise scenarios can produce negative net outcomes

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: How equity is valued when comparing offers
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Looks at the headline grant number (e.g., '$400K in RSU over 4 years') and treats it as equivalent to $100K/year in salary
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Models after-tax value at each vesting tranche, accounts for vesting schedule structure, discounts pre-IPO grants for liquidity risk, and compares net annual equity income
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Two offers with identical stated equity values can have dramatically different realized take-home value depending on tax treatment, vesting schedule, and liquidity

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Response to the 90-day post-departure exercise window
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Doesn't notice or ignores the exercise window clause; assumes they can 'deal with it later' if they ever leave
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Calculates total cash needed to exercise all vested options plus anticipated tax bill, and evaluates whether that is financially feasible — treats extended exercise windows as a meaningful compensation differentiator
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Candidates who cannot fund option exercise upon departure forfeit significant vested compensation; this is an avoidable but frequently unmodeled risk

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Understanding of ISO vs. NSO distinction
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Treats all 'stock options' as interchangeable; assumes options are always a simple buy-low-sell-high mechanism
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Knows ISO triggers AMT at exercise (not just at sale), understands that early exercise creates tax liability decoupled from liquidity, and consults a tax professional before any ISO exercise decision
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: ISO AMT exposure is the mechanism that caused mass bankruptcies in the 2000 dot-com crash; it is a real, recurring risk that naive employees repeatedly walk into

community_misconceptions.misconception: If my stock options are underwater (stock price below strike price), I simply don't exercise and I lose nothing
community_misconceptions.why_believed: For unexercised NSO options this is technically true — but it feels universally applicable to all option types
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: For ISO options that have already been early-exercised, AMT may have already been calculated on the spread at exercise time; if the stock subsequently drops, you still owe the AMT tax on a gain that no longer exists in the stock's current value
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Employees who early-exercise ISO options and then see the stock collapse face tax bills that can exceed the current value of their shares, and in extreme cases lead to bankruptcy

community_misconceptions.misconception: RSU is safer than options because you don't have to pay anything to receive it
community_misconceptions.why_believed: RSU requires no upfront capital and vests automatically — it feels unconditionally positive
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: RSU vesting is a taxable event at ordinary income rates; for pre-IPO RSU, a large accumulated balance at IPO can create a massive single-year tax liability, and if the company's stock drops after IPO lockup expires, the employee has already paid taxes on a higher value than they can now recover
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Employees who receive large pre-IPO RSU grants, pay ~50% tax at IPO vesting, and then hold shares that subsequently decline end up with less net value than the headline grant suggested — sometimes significantly less

community_misconceptions.misconception: The RSU or option value stated in your offer letter is your actual compensation
community_misconceptions.why_believed: The offer letter presents a specific dollar figure or share count, which anchors perception of total compensation
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: The stated value is pre-tax gross; actual take-home depends on tax bracket, state of residence, vesting schedule timing, stock price at vesting (for RSU), and whether the company achieves a liquidity event (for pre-IPO grants)
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Candidates accept offers based on inflated perceived compensation, then experience sticker shock at the actual after-tax, post-liquidity-risk value they realize

real_case_outcomes.situation: Employee joins a startup, receives NSO options with $5 strike price on 10,000 shares; company IPOs 4 years later at $25/share with all options vested
real_case_outcomes.decision: Employee exercises all 10,000 options at once in the IPO year, realizing $200,000 in gains
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Tax on $200,000 at ordinary income rates plus California state tax consumes approximately $100,000; plus $50,000 upfront exercise cost = $150,000 total outlay to net $50,000 from a $200,000 paper gain
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Exercising all options in a single year maximizes tax exposure; staggered annual exercise can reduce marginal rate and total tax burden — but requires planning before the IPO year

real_case_outcomes.situation: Employee joins a startup early and receives ISO options; exercises early to start the capital gains clock before IPO
real_case_outcomes.decision: Early exercises ISO options at a low strike price, anticipating IPO and long-term capital gains treatment
real_case_outcomes.outcome: If the company's stock subsequently collapses (as happened widely in 2000), the employee still owes AMT calculated on the spread at exercise time — tax bills can exceed the current value of the shares, leading to bankruptcy in the most severe cases
real_case_outcomes.lesson: ISO early exercise is a high-stakes tax strategy that requires professional advice and a credible exit scenario; it is not a universally beneficial optimization and carries catastrophic downside

psychological_barriers.trigger: New graduate receives an offer with equity and immediately asks 'how do I compare this to the other offer's salary?'
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Certainty bias — the candidate anchors to the concrete, guaranteed component (salary) and discounts the variable component (equity) because it feels speculative and hard to evaluate
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Candidate either ignores equity entirely in the comparison or treats the stated grant value as face-value equivalent to cash
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Reframe equity as a range of outcomes, not a single number: 'Model three scenarios — company fails (equity = $0), company performs like peers (equity = stated value after tax), company outperforms (equity = 3-5x stated value). Now which offer looks better across scenarios?'

psychological_barriers.trigger: Candidate at a pre-IPO startup asks 'should I take the lower base salary because the RSU is worth so much?'
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Narrative bias — the candidate is seduced by the compelling startup story and assigns high probability to the optimistic liquidity scenario, underweighting the base rate of startup failures
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Candidate accepts below-market base salary in exchange for equity that may never liquidate, treating the RSU value as near-certain future cash
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Ask the candidate: 'If I told you today that this company will never IPO or be acquired, would you still take the offer at this base salary?' If no, the equity discount is larger than they're willing to accept

psychological_barriers.trigger: Employee holds unexercised vested options after IPO and repeatedly defers the decision to exercise
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Regret aversion combined with status quo bias — exercising locks in a tax bill and feels like a commitment; not exercising feels like preserving optionality, even as the window to act shrinks
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Employee delays exercising year after year, misses optimal tax planning windows, and either forfeits options at expiration or exercises all at once in a high-tax year
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Reframe: 'Every year you don't partially exercise, you are making an active bet that the stock will rise enough to justify a higher tax bracket hit later. Is that bet intentional or just inertia?'

reframing_moves.original_framing: New graduates focus on base salary differences and treat equity as a bonus or afterthought
reframing_moves.reframe: In Silicon Valley, the prevailing view is that equity is the primary wealth-building mechanism and base salary is just 'enough to live on' — the real question is the quality and structure of the equity
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Shifts the candidate's optimization target from the certain-but-capped variable (salary) to the uncertain-but-uncapped variable (equity), prompting them to actually analyze the equity terms
reframing_moves.example_language: 硅谷、湾区的主流观点早就认为收入中股票期权为王，基本工资用来养养家就好

reframing_moves.original_framing: Employees assume equity is free upside with no downside — 'worst case I get nothing'
reframing_moves.reframe: The real worst case is not zero — it is a tax liability that exceeds the current value of your shares, as happened to thousands of engineers in 2000
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Replaces the comfortable 'free lottery ticket' mental model with an accurate risk model that includes negative outcomes, motivating due diligence on tax mechanics before acting
reframing_moves.example_language: 知道为啥2000年互联网大泡沫后无数程序员破产么？税！

reframing_moves.original_framing: Pre-IPO startup equity feels real because the offer letter states a specific dollar value
reframing_moves.reframe: Equity at a pre-IPO company is contingent on two independent events happening: the company achieving a liquidity event, AND you still being an employee (or having exercised options in time). Until both occur, the value is zero.
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Breaks the single-number anchor and replaces it with a two-condition probability model, forcing the candidate to separately assess both the company's exit probability and their own tenure probability
reframing_moves.example_language: 无论是RSU/Option, 只要公司没有办法上市或者被收购，或者你在此之前已经离开，这些RSU/Option则分文不值
